accuracy.evidence: Checked the facts the lesson relies on: the England multiplication tables check allows 6 seconds per question (STA, MTC assessment framework), used as the line for 'slow'; the smaller-from-larger subtraction bug is documented by Brown and Burton (1978) and VanLehn (1990), and Leo's answers follow it exactly (72-38 gives 46, 51-24 gives 33, 83-47 gives 44, while 58-23 and 96-41 need no exchange and come out right); every times-table answer and correction (7 x 8 = 56, 7 x 9 = 63) was recomputed. The five-day race is labelled on the canvas and in the adult text as a picture of the idea, not data.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the real slips in choosing what to practise: counting only wrong answers (the prediction 'Only the 2 she got wrong', and Check flags the slow right ones), deciding a whole topic is hard when one step is (Leo prediction 'Subtraction: all of it'), redoing the whole test ('Same quiz again' gives 4 of 10 tries on the hard part), staying with easy practice because it feels good, and either practising a fixed fact for ever or dropping it (recheck sort and challenge). These match the EEF metacognition guidance and the deliberate-practice literature on aiming practice at weaknesses.

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanics belong to this topic: marking rows of a result sheet by both correctness and time against a 6-second line, locating the faulty step inside worked column subtractions, filling a 10-slot practice plan with a hard-part meter and coverage rule, a two-plan fluency race driven by how many tries land on weak facts, and re-sorting new results by a drag-to-box card. None of these is a relabel of another lab, including flagdelib and flagonenew, and the shingle gate keeps it under 30% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner finds each idea by doing it: Check only passes once slow right answers are marked too; tapping each wrong sum's step reveals the same exchange slip three times before the plan question; the meter and Same quiz again show how few tries a full redo puts on the hard part; Next day shows Plan B's bars reach the fluent line by day 4 while Plan A stays under it; the recheck moves 6 x 7 out and brings 7 x 9 in, so the hard part visibly moves. The done text only confirms.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong answer the lab disproves: 'Only the 2 she got wrong' (Check then names 6 x 7 at 11 s as a hard part), 'Subtraction: all of it' (three wrong sums share one step and two non-exchange sums are right), and 'Plan A: the whole quiz again' (its bars never reach fluent in 5 days). The reveal line reports whether the prediction was right.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Each wrong option is tagged and gets feedback for its slip: right-but-slow still counts, redoing everything spends tries on what is known, easy practice feels good but changes little, skipping the hard part keeps it hard, the hard part is often one step, daily practice on a fluent fact is wasted, and never looking again lets it fade. Inside the steps, marking an easy fact, missing a wrong or slow one, choosing the tens step, a short plan, a plan with too few hard tries, a missing hard fact, and each wrong box all get specific messages.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and plain words (wrong, slow, step, swap a ten for ten ones) and pass the family kid limit in validate_lessons.py; key terms are explained where they appear (slow means you had to work it out). On-canvas prompts are one line each ('Card 2 of 5: which box?'). The adult text names the research and passes its limit.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph carries one move (find wrong and slow, find the step, plan, recheck); each adult paragraph gives evidence, the bug example, the common mistakes or the lab outline with related lessons. The content gate found no filler phrases and the explanation is under 12% the same as every other lesson, including 464 Deliberate practice and 1074 One new thing at a time.

mobile.evidence: Checked 390 px screenshots in light and dark for every step before and after Show me, and 1200 px desktop: the 10 quiz rows fit with answer, right/wrong, seconds and HARD tag on one line; Leo's step choices are stacked full-width so their text stays at full size; the 10 plan slots and 8 fact cards fit in two grids; the two plan charts sit side by side with readable fact labels; the recheck bins split their titles over two lines so nothing is clipped. Empty slots use a light fill with dark numbers so they read in dark mode.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin: one toggle per quiz row with aria-pressed and a label giving the answer, right or wrong, and seconds, plus Check my marks; the three step buttons and the plan question; Add buttons for all 8 facts with Same quiz again, Clear plan and Check plan; Next day and the race question; and Keep practising / Easy now, labelled with the card being sorted, as an alternative to dragging. The canvas aria-label states each result in words, and the walk gate's axe run is clean in both themes.
